Description: anti-pattern — merging basemap and application data into one tileset
prompt: I want my roads, water, labels, and my own delivery-zone polygons all in a single vector tileset so the map only hits one source. What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer – don’t merge everything into one tileset unless you have a very special offline‑only use case.**  
For virtually every web‑map you’ll get better flexibility, lower maintenance cost, and fewer licensing headaches by keeping the basemap (roads, water, labels, etc.) as one source and your delivery‑zone polygons as a second source.

Below is the recommended “two‑source” pattern, followed by a concise description of the pipeline you would use **only if you really must create a single combined vector‑tile set** (e.g., an air‑gapped kiosk or a proof‑of‑concept that cannot make a second network request).

---

## 1️⃣ Why the “one source” idea isn’t a performance win

| Reason | What happens if you merge |
|--------|---------------------------|
| **Tile‑generation cost** | Every time your delivery‑zone data changes you must rebuild the entire basemap tileset (planet‑scale or large regional extracts). That is orders of magnitude slower than just re‑publishing a small custom tileset. |
| **Loss of basemap upgrades** | You can’t swap a newer OpenStreetMap (OSM) style, add new layers, or fix bugs without rebuilding the whole combined set. |
| **Attribution & licensing** | You become a redistributor of OSM data and must carry its attribution in the tiles you serve. Keeping the basemap separate lets the provider handle that for you. |
| **No rendering penalty for multiple sources** | MapLibre fetches all declared sources in parallel; there is no per‑source overhead that would be avoided by merging. |
| **Layer‑order & styling flexibility** | With separate sources you can insert your polygons before or after the basemap’s label layer, change their style on the fly, or turn them on/off without touching the basemap tiles. |

Because of these points, the **standard production pattern** is:

```json
{
  "sources": {
    "basemap": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "https://{provider}/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"   // or a TileJSON URL
    },
    "delivery-zones": {
      "type": "vector",          // or "geojson" if the dataset is small
      "url": "https://my.cdn.com/delivery-zones.pmtiles"   // see PMTiles below
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    /* basemap layers … */
    /* insert your polygon layer before the first symbol layer so labels stay on top */
    {
      "id": "delivery-zones-fill",
      "type": "fill",
      "source": "delivery-zones",
      "source-layer": "delivery_zones",   // name you gave when tiling
      "paint": { "fill-color": "#ff6600", "fill-opacity": 0.4 }
    },
    {
      "id": "delivery-zones-outline",
      "type": "line",
      "source": "delivery-zones",
      "source-layer": "delivery_zones",
      "paint": { "line-color": "#ff6600", "line-width": 2 }
    }
  ]
}
```

*If your delivery‑zone dataset is under the “sweet‑spot” for GeoJSON (< 2 MB / < 5 k features), you could even use a `geojson` source instead of a tiled one and skip the tile‑generation step entirely.*

---

## 2️⃣ When a single combined tileset **is** justified

Typical scenarios:

| Scenario | Why a single file makes sense |
|----------|------------------------------|
| **Offline kiosk / air‑gapped device** – the map must work without any network connection. |
| **Demo / proof‑of‑concept** – you want a single archive to hand to a reviewer. |
| **Very small region** – you are serving a tiny city‑scale map where the basemap extract is only a few megabytes and you want to ship everything as one PMTiles file. |

If you fall into one of those cases, here’s the **high‑level pipeline** you would follow. The skill does **not** ask you to write the full build script; we only name the tools and point you to their docs.

### Step‑by‑step overview

1. **Obtain the OSM base data** you need.  
   * For a whole planet or a large region, download an `.osm.pbf` from a provider such as Geofabrik or MapLibre’s own extracts.  
   * For a tiny city you can use the same source; the size difference is handled later by the tiler.

2. **Add your delivery‑zone polygons** to that OSM extract.  
   * Convert your polygons to **GeoJSON** (or **FlatGeobuf** if you prefer a binary format).  
   * Use a tool like **`ogr2ogr`** (GDAL) or **`tippecanoe`**’s `--add` flag to merge the GeoJSON into the OSM PBF, preserving OSM tags if you need them.  
   * Example (conceptual only):  
     ```bash
     ogr2ogr -f "OSM" merged.osm.pbf base.osm.pbf delivery_zones.geojson
     ```

3. **Tile the combined dataset**. Two widely used, production‑grade options are:

   * **Tippecanoe** – great for static GeoJSON → MBTiles/PMTiles pipelines.  
     * Docs: <https://github.com/felt/tippecanoe>  
     * Typical command (conceptual):  
       ```bash
       tippecanoe \
         --output=combined.pmtiles \
         --layer=basemap \
         --layer=delivery_zones \
         --maximum-zoom=14 \
         --minimum-zoom=5 \
         merged.osm.pbf
       ```
     * Use `--force` and `--drop-densest-as-needed` to keep the tile size under the 500 KB per tile limit that browsers handle comfortably.

   * **Planetiler** – a Java/Kotlin pipeline that can ingest OSM PBFs, apply custom processing, and output vector tiles (MBTiles or PMTiles).  
     * Docs: <https://github.com/onthegomap/planetiler>  
     * It lets you write a small Kotlin program where you can assign a distinct `layer` name to your delivery‑zone polygons, apply simplification, and control zoom‑level detail.

   * Both tools can output **PMTiles** (a single‑file archive) which MapLibre can read directly via the `pmtiles` protocol (`url: "pmtiles://https://my.cdn.com/combined.pmtiles"`). See the skill **maplibre-pmtiles-patterns** for wiring details.

4. **Host the tile archive**.  
   * Upload the `.pmtiles` file to a CDN or static‑file host that supports range requests (e.g., Cloudflare R2, AWS S3 + CloudFront, Netlify).  
   * Ensure CORS headers allow `*` or your domain, because MapLibre will request byte ranges.

5. **Reference it in your style**.  
   ```json
   "sources": {
     "combined": {
       "type": "vector",
       "url": "pmtiles://https://my.cdn.com/combined.pmtiles"
     }
   }
   ```
   * Use the `source-layer` names you gave in step 3 (`basemap`, `delivery_zones`) when defining layers.

6. **Test the tile size**.  
   * Open the style in the MapLibre GL JS Playground or a local dev build.  
   * Inspect network requests: each tile should be well under 500 KB (ideally < 200 KB) to avoid long pauses on mobile.

### Quick checklist of the tools you’ll need

| Tool | What it does | Docs / install |
|------|--------------|----------------|
| **`ogr2ogr` (GDAL)** | Convert/merge your polygons into OSM PBF (or directly to GeoJSON) | <https://gdal.org/programs/ogr2ogr.html> |
| **Tippecanoe** | Fast, command‑line vector‑tile generator for GeoJSON/OSM → MBTiles/PMTiles | <https://github.com/felt/tippecanoe> |
| **Planetiler** | Java/Kotlin pipeline for large‑scale OSM tiling with custom processing | <https://github.com/onthegomap/planetiler> |
| **PMTiles** (library & protocol) | Serve a single‑file tile archive via HTTP range requests | <https://github.com/protomaps/PMTiles> |
| **MapLibre GL JS** | Consume the `pmtiles://` URL in a style | <https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js-docs/api/> |

---

## 3️⃣ TL;DR – Recommended workflow for most apps

1. **Pick a hosted vector basemap** (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, your own TileServer).  
2. **Add your delivery‑zone data as a separate source**:  
   * If < 5 k features → `geojson` source (no tiling needed).  
   * If larger → generate a small vector tileset (Tippecanoe → PMTiles) and reference it as a second `vector` source.  
3. **Insert your polygon layers before the first label layer** so labels stay on top.  
4. **Deploy** – no need to rebuild the basemap when your polygons change.

Only go to the “single combined tileset” pipeline when you truly cannot make a second network request (offline, kiosk, demo). In all other cases, the two‑source pattern gives you:

* **Zero extra build work** when your polygons change (just republish the small custom tileset).  
* **Instant basemap upgrades** (just point to a newer style URL).  
* **Clear attribution handling** (basemap provider keeps its own attribution).  
* **Full styling flexibility** (you can turn your layer on/off, recolor it, or query it without touching the basemap).

---

### Want to see a concrete example?

- **Two‑source style** tutorial: <https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-gl-js-docs/tree/main/examples/custom-data>  
- **PMTiles + Tippecanoe** pattern: <https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-pmtiles-patterns>  

Feel free to ask if you need help wiring the `pmtiles://` URL into your style or deciding whether your delivery‑zone dataset is small enough for a plain GeoJSON source. Happy mapping!

Description: explicit — vector tiles for a restylable basemap, not raw performance
prompt: I want to offer both a light and dark theme for my basemap, switchable at runtime, without hosting two separate sets of tiles. What tile type should my basemap use?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Use **`vector` **tiles for the basemap.**  

### Why a vector source lets you toggle light / dark at runtime

| Aspect | Vector tiles | Raster tiles |
|--------|--------------|--------------|
| **Styling** | The geometry and attributes are delivered once (as compact MVT/MLT). All visual properties (fill colour, line width, label colour, etc.) are applied **client‑side** by the style JSON. You can swap the style (or just change a few paint/layout values) without fetching a new set of tiles. | The image for each tile is already rendered with a specific colour scheme. To get a different theme you must serve a completely separate raster tile set (e.g. `…/light/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` vs `…/dark/{z}/{x}/{y}.png`). |
| **Bandwidth** | One tile request per viewport, regardless of theme. | Two full tile sets → double the storage and bandwidth if you keep both. |
| **Interactivity** | Features stay queryable (`queryRenderedFeatures`, click/hover, etc.) because the raw geometry is still in the client. | No feature data – only pixels, so you lose click/hover, label search, etc. |
| **Future‑proofing** | You can add more themes (high‑contrast, colour‑blind, night‑mode) simply by loading a different style JSON or toggling a few paint values. | Every new theme means a new raster generation pipeline. |
| **Offline / cache** | One set of tiles can be cached and reused for any theme. | You would need to cache both sets, doubling the storage requirement. |

### How to implement the switch

1. **Serve a single vector tile source** (TileJSON, PMTiles, XYZ, etc.).  
   ```json
   // tile source definition (shared by both themes)
   {
     "type": "vector",
     "url": "https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"
   }
   ```

2. **Create two style JSONs** – one “light” and one “dark”.  
   Both reference the same source name, but each defines its own `paint`/`layout` values (background colour, road colours, label colours, etc.).  
   ```json
   // light-style.json
   {
     "version": 8,
     "sources": { "basemap": { "type": "vector", "url": "..."} },
     "layers": [
       { "id": "background", "type": "background", "paint": { "background-color": "#f8f9fa" } },
       /* other layers with light colours */
     ]
   }
   ```

   ```json
   // dark-style.json
   {
     "version": 8,
     "sources": { "basemap": { "type": "vector", "url": "..."} },
   ```
